newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - EMU convergence not guaranteed by criteria.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - EMU convergence not guaranteed by criteria.

text.p: The rules of entry into Europe's single currency club may bring the continent's economies into the same cycle but their success is not guaranteed, a Reuters survey showed on Thursday.

Only seven of the contributors to the survey, carried out on April 14 and 15, said they believed the entry requirements for European economic and monetary union (EMU) were "very likely" to promote economic convergence. Thirteen said it was "likely" and 12 said it was "quite likely".
Four respondents said the entry rules were "unlikely" to promote convergence and three said they were "very unlikely" under any circumstances.

"I don't agree that the criteria were designed to promote economic convergence. They were designed to exclude countries in southern Europe," said Jean-Paul Fitoussi of the OFCE, a French private forecasting organisation.

Others said the criteria ignored economic trends including wages, money supply and unemployment, which can be equally or more important than the inflation, gross domestic product(GDP), budget deficit and debt levels upon which the criteria are based.
Most of the forecasters who said the Maastricht targets would promote convergence said it would come only hand-in-hand with implementation of the EMU stability pact.
Under the terms of the pact, formalised last December, any country which runs a budget deficit of more than three percent of GDP will face sanctions and fines.
Exemptions will only apply where countries are forced to overspend by circumstances beyond their control or where economic growth contracts by two percent or more a year.
Some believe the convergence targets will create a vicious circle of fiscal restraint and low growth.
"Unless you have five percent nominal growth...the criteria will be very difficult to achieve," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
The analysts were asked about the percentage likelihood of a major crisis hitting EMU within the first two years of its existence. The average finding was 24 percent, unchanged from March.
"There will only be a currency crisis if there is a major political crisis," said Marion Swoboda, economist at Credit Suisse in Zurich. "Most people do not think there is much chance of that."
Others said they would increase their forecasts of a major currency crisis within two years if a broad-based EMU were the only option available.

"If the currency area expands there is a risk of instability. Central banks are looking at the demand for money. With a broader base, the stability of money may collapse and the ability to monitor it as a reliable indicator breaks down," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
